title: The Ohio Lucky Seven and the armory dances
summary: A manager rents small-town armories for the kid band to run its own dances, and each member takes home about $30 a weekend, which wins over his grandparents.

bands.name: Monk Mollencup and His Society Orchestra

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Now, the first real band you played with was Monk Mollencup and then this group that you went to Hamilton Lake with you called the Ohio Lucky Seven --

Yes, we -- getting started is now after that lake job, because this time, we got a manager which was the trombone player's brother and he said -- "Why don't you let me manage you kids?" "You kids", I think he said, "are good". And, "you need somebody to back you up." And, so, we let him take the band over. And, so, he thought of a very brilliant idea. In Ohio, around

where I came from, there were hundreds of vacant armories. Every little town had an armory and they always had a nice big drill floor, which is good for dancing. So, he said - "Why can't we put out some hand-bills and publicity and we can rent these armories very, very cheap and put our own dances on?" Which, he did. And, here we are kids, making - you know - for weekends, like Friday night and Saturday and some days on Sunday, we kids were taking home $30.00 a piece - my God, that was a lot of money, you know.

That was a pile of money. My grandparents were delighted that when I did that, I'd bring the money home, of course, and help with everything and they thought it was a good idea for me to be in the music business. But, before, they absolutely didn't want me to be a musician.
This armory business actually - probably started right about the same time you went to Hamilton Lake the first time - didn't it?
